articles.summary_long:
It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes.

As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils. articles.summary_long:
Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet . Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, this inspired composited scene covers the dim outer planet, largest moon Triton , and faint system of rings.

From just beyond Neptune's orbit, the interplanetary perspective looks back toward the Sun, capturing the planet and Triton as thin sunlit crescents . Cirrus clouds and a dark band circle Neptune's south polar region, with a cloudy vortex above the pole itself . Parts of the very faint ring system along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture.

Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager's view of the magnificent Neptunian system . Still cruising in 2026, the Voyager 2 spacecraft is now in interstellar space .

A creative rut can last a weekend or a year and a half, and the usual fix in photography, buying something new, stops working eventually. For one photographer coming out of a long slump, the way back turned out to be a photo book that had sat in an online basket for years. Along the way, his video camera slips out of the tripod clamp into a puddle.

Cameras like it didn't exist before 2018, and they changed what solo filmmaking looks like, while stills cameras like the Sony A7 he's filming on have looked the same forever. His conclusion, which he says took about 15 years to land, is that when you're in front of something you care about in the right light, you could be shooting with a potato and still be happy. When you aren't, an interesting camera won't get you a photo you like anyway.

What finally started pulling him out was a Harry Gruyaert book that had sat in his online basket for years. Other people's work no longer gives him directions to follow, the way it did when he started. Like James says in the video, I too really like books.

articles.title: Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green
articles.summary: Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric.
articles.summary_short: Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric.
articles.summary_long:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends. The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19.

articles.summary_long:
Jack and Nathan, the duo behind the hit VR game Yeeps, took the stage at Maker Faire Bay Area 2026 to share their origin story, tracing a decade-long journey that began when they discovered, within the first few days of their freshman year of high school, that they were both making games. After childhoods spent with Lego, Minecraft, and early Scratch projects, the pair began staying after school to build together, starting with simple titles like Barrels and Asteroid Escape . They were candid about their missteps in those early days: an ambitious empire-building game called Imperium never made it past a pile of spreadsheets, a lesson they summed up as “start stuff you can finish quickly” and save dream projects for later.

Discovering VR changed everything–and brought “save for later” into “get started.” Their first VR prototype reimagined Asteroid Escape with a gigantic space worm, followed by Overboard , a shark-fighting game that taught them to play-test, market, and finally ship a project on Steam. Their next game, Gods of Gravity , was one of the first real-time strategy games built for VR. More than two years after launch, their studio, Trass Games , has grown to about 25 people, and the game’s spirit has spilled into the real world through a Yeeps plush maker kit and countless fan-made costumes, gadgets, and crafts.

Crediting their parents, in the audience at MFBA, as their earliest supporters and best critics, the founders closed with advice for young makers and their parents: start building early, make it social, work consistently, and don’t wait for a job or a degree to give you permission. The brought this advice into reality at Maker Faire by hosting a workshop in which kids could build their own felt plushie Yeeps characters, accessorize them with DIY gizmos, and launch them into the sky. Jennifer Blakeslee keeps the Global Maker Faire program running smoothly and has been a maker at Maker Faire since 2011.

articles.title: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers
articles.summary: Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star.
articles.summary_short: Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star.
articles.summary_long:
Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward.

The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star. Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy.

articles.title: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up
articles.summary: Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean.

articles.summary_long:
Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

articles.title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects.
articles.summary_short: Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. articles.summary_long:
Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.” Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. "The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark said. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing." That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset.

articles.title: A Doctored Photo Left People Recalling Details of a Balloon Ride That Never Happened
articles.summary: Eight of their 20 subjects, 40%, reported partial or clear false beliefs or memories. They are arguing about how much of a report has to be invented before it counts as a false memory.
articles.summary_short: Eight of their 20 subjects, 40%, reported partial or clear false beliefs or memories. They are arguing about how much of a report has to be invented before it counts as a false memory.
articles.summary_long:
Twenty adults in Wellington, New Zealand, sat down with a booklet of four grayscale prints, each one 150 mm square inside a thin black border, and by the end of the third interview, half of them were describing a childhood hot air balloon ride that had never happened. A partial false memory meant the subject consistently elaborated on the photo, reporting feelings or who was present, without indicating a memory of taking the ride itself. By the third interview, 4 subjects had clear false memories and 6 had partial ones.

A clear false memory meant describing the balloon ride itself with detail beyond the photograph; a partial one meant elaborating on the picture, the feelings, who was there, without indicating a memory of taking the flight. Eight of their 20 subjects, 40%, reported partial or clear false beliefs or memories. In a 2005 follow-up , published under the title "Actually, a Picture Is Worth Less Than 45 Words," they gave 44 subjects the same balloon ride, half of them as a doctored photograph and half as a personalized 45-word written description.

At the final interview, 82% of the narrative group reported at least some information about the ride, images or memories, against 50% of the photo group. A picture of someone standing at a microphone tells you nothing about whether they are still breathing. They are arguing about how much of a report has to be invented before it counts as a false memory.

La nouvelle version est disponible pour tous depuis le 9 novembre 2026 , date à laquelle Imagen a aussi lancé son offre Black Friday , valable jusqu’au 4 décembre.

La nouvelle version est disponible pour tous depuis le 9 novembre 2026 , date à laquelle Imagen a aussi lancé son offre Black Friday , valable jusqu’au 4 décembre.
articles.summary_long:
Le service, connu des photographes de mariage et d’événementiel pour appliquer leur style de retouche à des galeries entières dans Lightroom, devient plus complet avec la sortie du module Intelligent Studio : tri, retouche manuelle et assistant IA sont désormais réunis dans la même application. La nouvelle version est disponible pour tous depuis le 9 novembre 2026 , date à laquelle Imagen a aussi lancé son offre Black Friday , valable jusqu’au 4 décembre. Pour piloter cet éditeur, Imagen mise sur un Assistant à qui l’on écrit en langage courant .

Imagen insiste sur un point : l’Assistant ne génère aucune image . Imagen peut faire un premier passage pendant l’import , en gardant la meilleure image de chaque scène ou en réduisant la série à un nombre de photos défini. Un test complet d’Imagen et son nouvel outil Intelligent Studio est en cours à la rédaction.

Jusqu’au 4 décembre 2026, le premier mois de l’abonnement Limitless mensuel passe à 5 € au lieu de 139 €. Les abonnés Limitless obtiennent 50 % de remise sur cette même boutique et deux essais de tri gratuits. A noter qu’Imagen propose également 1500 éditions IA gratuites en créant son compte .

articles.title: Hacker son appareil photo avec l’IA : Caira veut rendre la pratique officielle
articles.summary: Alors que des photographes modifient le firmware de leurs boîtiers Sony, Sigma ou Nikon avec Claude ou ChatGPT, la start-up londonienne Camera Intelligence prépare un environnement de développement officiel, Creative Sandbox , pour son appareil photo hybride Caira . Ouverture au public prévue en 2027, après un hackathon réservé à une vingtaine de participants.

articles.summary_long:
Alors que des photographes modifient le firmware de leurs boîtiers Sony, Sigma ou Nikon avec Claude ou ChatGPT, la start-up londonienne Camera Intelligence prépare un environnement de développement officiel, Creative Sandbox , pour son appareil photo hybride Caira . Ouverture au public prévue en 2027, après un hackathon réservé à une vingtaine de participants. C’est précisément sur ce risque que Camera Intelligence veut se positionner.

Il fonctionne sous Camera Intelligence OS, un système maison basé sur Linux. Selon Caira, Creative Sandbox sera un espace isolé au sein de ce système , où les propriétaires pourront créer leurs propres fonctions avec leurs outils de code par IA, sans risquer de rendre l’appareil inutilisable . Camera Intelligence présente sa démarche dans une vidéo de lancement : Pour préparer le terrain, Caira souhaite organiser un hackaton, le Holiday Camera Hack , en décembre dans les locaux londoniens de la société, pour une vingtaine de photographes, vidéastes, journalistes et développeurs, sans compétence en code exigée.

Le gagnant repartira avec un appareil Caira, et les places seront confirmées d’ici le 27 novembre ; date exacte et lieu restent à préciser. Ces travaux doivent permettent à Caira d’affiner le Creative Sandbox avant son ouverture à tous les propriétaires, prévue en 2027. Et l’appareil peut gagner de nouvelles fonctions sans qu’on doive racheter un boîtier.

articles.title: Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland’s Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson
articles.summary: Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country.
articles.summary_short: Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country.
articles.summary_long:
Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson , Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it.

articles.summary: A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

articles.summary_long:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate. In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was.

Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat , the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world. As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

articles.title: Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
articles.summary: The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara ’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center , where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown.

articles.summary_long:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara ’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center , where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner ’s galleries. Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake .

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.” The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

articles.title: ‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists
articles.summary: In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. Black history is American history.” We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem.
articles.summary_short: In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. Black history is American history.” We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem.
articles.summary_long:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. For quilter Rosy Petri , Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery .

The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network ( WCQN ), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak ’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. “All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement.

“This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.” We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release , Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers .

articles.summary: Above, “ Tethered robot runs on sand ” by UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering , CC BY 4.0 What makes a project a robot? Is it advanced electronics or powerful computers?

articles.summary_long:
Above, “ Tethered robot runs on sand ” by UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering , CC BY 4.0 What makes a project a robot? Is it advanced electronics or powerful computers? Engineers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering reject all these things.

They’ve built a six-legged inflatable robot designed to operate where electronic ones can’t. So have they, since they developed the first version in 2022. They ended up borrowing ideas from steam engines to make it possible.

Sam Freeman is an Online Editor at Make. He builds interactive art, collects retro tech, and tries to get robots to make things for him. Learn more at samtastic.co , or on socials @samdiyfreeman.

articles.title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
articles.summary: A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean. On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines.

articles.summary_long:
À plus de 5 000 années-lumière de la Terre, des astronomes ont identifié l'origine de mystérieuses impulsions radio qui se répètent toutes les huit minutes. Leur découverte ne permet pas seulement de mieux comprendre une famille d'objets encore énigmatiques. Depuis 2010, il envoie régulièrement de fascinants clichés du Soleil vers notre Planète.

L'étude de notre Soleil permet de tester certaines de nos théories sur les étoiles et, inversement, l'étude d'étoiles similaires au Soleil permet d'en apprendre plus sur lui. Les phénomènes éruptifs à la surface du Soleil peuvent varier considérablement. Certains se limitent à une éruption solaire, d'autres s'accompagnent d'une éjection de matière solaire – appelée éjection de masse coronale (EMC) – tandis que certains impliquent des structures complexes en mouvement, associées à des modifications des lignes de champ magnétique qui s'élèvent en boucles dans l'atmosphère solaire, la couronne.

Le 19 juillet 2012, une éruption solaire a combiné ces trois manifestations. le Soleil a offert aux observateurs l'un de ses spectaculaires phénomènes magnétiques : ce que l'on appelle la « pluie coronale ». C'est la première fois que des pulsations radio sont détectées dans une telle association entre une naine blanche et une étoile de type solaire.

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces. According to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ.

This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. This image shows CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. AnJ The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star.

But why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

Around 4.5 billion years ago, when our Solar System hadnât fully formed yet, ultraviolet light from the Sun blew apart carbon monoxide molecules at the outer edges of the protoplanetary disk of gas and dust.

They eventually reformed with hydrogen to make âregularâ water. And some of those wavelengths were particularly good at breaking apart carbon monoxide molecules that had formed with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. articles.title: 3 Things That Make a Photo Look Cinematic, and Color Grading Isn't One
articles.summary: Color grading plays a much smaller part in why a frame feels like a still from a movie than most people assume, and the bigger factors are things you can start working on the next time you pick up a camera. Films stack shadow, light, shadow, light across the frame so the subject separates from whatever sits behind it.

articles.summary_long:
Teal shadows and orange highlights have become shorthand for a cinematic photo, and plenty of presets promise that look in a single click. Color grading plays a much smaller part in why a frame feels like a still from a movie than most people assume, and the bigger factors are things you can start working on the next time you pick up a camera. Light carries most of the look, and Kent shoots much of the video in heavy mist to show the kind he means.

Kent points out that once you notice that gentle transition, you'll find it in nearly every scene of every film you watch, and he still recommends learning to work in harsh sun, since soft pockets of light exist even then if you know where to look. Kent ties it to direction, since light coming from the side builds depth, and depth is the hard-to-name quality that makes a movie frame feel like you could step into it. Films stack shadow, light, shadow, light across the frame so the subject separates from whatever sits behind it.

Kent also argues for settling when you have to. Photographers don't control the light the way a film crew does, so two of the three, such as soft light on a subject or directional light on one, can still look cinematic, and you can tip the odds by moving yourself relative to the light, such as putting your subject's back to the sun. Kent filmed the video on a misty morning, so its own footage shows the soft light he's describing.

Focus on a face at the long end, zoom back to wide, and the face is still sharp. articles.title: Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes
articles.summary: Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre . A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.” The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux.
articles.summary_short: Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre . A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.” The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux.
articles.summary_long:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre . A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.” The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown.

And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks. Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?” In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. Perhaps they are trees of the future.” Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London.

articles.title: Vhils and Marcelo Cidade Cloak a São Paulo Colonial Building in Silver Thermal Blankets
articles.summary: “A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention.
articles.summary_short: “A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention.
articles.summary_long:
“A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention. In this sense, disappearance can begin before demolition,” says a statement about a recent collaboration between Alexandre Farto (a.k.a.

The monumental project at Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 2878 in Pinheiros, São Paulo, is a meditation on this sentiment as it considers how architecture and the seemingly mundane fixtures of city life shape our understanding of a place. Titled “2878,” the site-specific installation envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. Both drawing attention to the building and masking its real condition, the metallic blankets prompt questions about how we care for places and spaces.

As passersby walk past, the installation mirrors their silhouettes as faint reflections, while the surface’s color and light shift depending on the time of day. The collaborative intervention also evokes Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s “ Wrapped Reichstag ” and the early years of Andy Warhol’s Factory , in which silver paint and tin foil covered the walls of the artist’s New York studio. Warhol was interested in transience and the attention that comes with fame, concerns we see echoed and translated into broader conversations about public space, collective memory, and urban life in “2878.” Find more from Vhils and Cidade on their Instagrams.

articles.title: Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
articles.summary: As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian ’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits , the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil.
articles.summary_short: As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian ’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits , the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil.
articles.summary_long:
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian ’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits , the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. “I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal.

He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.” Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says.

Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process. Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

Publié le 18 novembre 2026, le manifeste de Numeum, intitulé « Faire de la France et de l’Europe une puissance numérique », place l’investissement, les compétences et l’autonomie stratégique au centre de ses priorités pour le prochain quinquennat. L’organisation, présidée par Mehdi Houas, fédère près de 2 500 entreprises du numérique représentant 85 % du chiffre d’affaires du secteur. Pour Numeum, la capacité du pays à développer ses propres technologies constitue un enjeu de compétitivité industrielle, mais aussi d’autonomie stratégique face aux grandes puissances technologiques.

La première proposition concerne le financement de la recherche et de l’innovation. Numeum souhaite porter les dépenses françaises de recherche et développement à 4 % du PIB d’ici 2035, contre 2,2 % selon ses données. Cet écart d’investissement constitue, selon Numeum, un frein à la capacité de la France à développer et industrialiser les innovations nécessaires à sa compétitivité.

Numeum souhaite faire de la commande publique un levier de développement de l’industrie numérique française et européenne. À l’échelle européenne, Numeum appelle à la création d’un pacte de compétitivité numérique destiné à renforcer la capacité des entreprises du continent à rivaliser avec les acteurs américains et asiatiques. Le syndicat entend ainsi inscrire l’investissement technologique, le développement des compétences et la souveraineté numérique parmi les priorités du prochain quinquennat.

articles.summary: When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. articles.summary_long:
When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars , "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, new simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars .

However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. Whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. Artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core.

Kornmesser Based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses. For more information, check out his website .

articles.title: Searching for Elusive Signals in the Cosmic Microwave Background from the South Pole
articles.summary: If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. But there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode.
articles.summary_short: If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. But there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode.
articles.summary_long:
As the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe. (Credit : NASA / WMAP Science Team) But there's also another way of studying the CMB. Gravitational lensing by intervening matter like galaxy clusters created this B-mode polarization.

If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. Next to the South Pole Telescope is the Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization (BICEP) array. BICEP was built to measure the B-mode polarization of the CMB that come directly from quantum gravity.

Members of the BICEP team in front of BICEP. But there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode. In 2014, the BICEP2 team presented a paper to their peers showing that they had detected B-mode polarization indicating a gravitational wave signal from inflation.

Today’s image captures a piece of the Sun ’s chromosphere , the layer of the Sun ’s atmosphere above its surface where the temperature rises .

This is potentially due to energy from the swirling magnetic fields extending up through the Sun’s atmosphere. Those same magnetic fields can twist and snap , releasing light and energetic particles as a solar flare . The H-alpha filter used for today’s image captures light from energized hydrogen atoms as they travel off the Sun’s surface during a flare on May 14, 2025.

articles.summary_long:
NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design.

Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.

The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. Future Engineers administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate. articles.summary: The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. articles.summary_short: The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. This year’s space agency partners are: Angola National Space Programme Management Office (GGPEN), Bahrain Space Agency, Brazilian Space Agency (AEB), CSA (Canadian Space Agency), ESA (European Space Agency), ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation), Italian Space Agency, JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Center of the United Arab Emirates, National Space Activities Commission of Argentina (CONAE), Nigeria’s National Space Research and Development Agency, Paraguayan Space Agency, Senegalese Space Studies Agency, Spanish Space Agency, Turkish Space Agency, and UK Space Agency.
articles.summary_long:
14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world. The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science. Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

The challenge provides an opportunity for hands-on experience with NASA science, mobilizing an engaged global community of technologists and space science enthusiasts to answer questions that benefit humanity and drive exploration. “The Space Apps Challenge invites people with many different skillsets to leverage NASA’s gold-standard datasets to address real challenges facing us here on Earth and in space,” said Amy Kaminski, engagement branch chief, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We’re thrilled to see more than 180,000 people tackling these challenges and helping to accelerate our ability to find solutions.” Challenges also feature data from 17 international space agency partners, all Artemis Accord signatories.

articles.summary_long:
The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂. As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important. AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions.

The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes. The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors. The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology.

These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew. Proposals should also demonstrate a pathway to continuous model updating as new empirical data become available, reflecting the iterative nature of a true digital twin. A new album from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory collects snapshots of baby stars across the galaxy and beyond and transforms that data into sound. Four new sonifications use data of stars that are actively forming, captured by Chandra and other NASA telescopes By studying places in the universe where stars are currently being born and young stars are present, astronomers can better understand the lifecycle of all stars, including our own Sun. One of the new sonifications combines Chandra’s data with optical data from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, as well as infrared views from NASA’s James Webb and retired Spitzer space telescopes.

In the sonified version of the Chandra data, these stars are twinkling sounds, while the diffuse X-ray emission is mapped to pure high tones. Chandra reveals infant stars that violently flare and produce X-rays. Infrared data from Webb provides views of the cloud’s regions of gas and dust.

The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. The sonification program is led by the Chandra X-ray Center (CXC). If everything is soft, background and all, it's camera shake. If the background is crisp and the subject isn't, the subject moved. According to Netflix's Tudum , the film arrived on the service on Nov.

The official trailer, above, moves from fashion sittings and celebrity portraits to protest footage, contact sheets, and Avedon himself at work in the studio. "Richard Avedon was an artist whose work continues to resonate not only because of the extraordinary images he created, but because of the humanity and curiosity behind them," Howard said. Much of Avedon's own voice comes from interviews Helen Whitney recorded for her American Masters film Richard Avedon: Darkness and Light , according to The Art Newspaper's review from Cannes .

Avedon stripped his best-known portraits down to a person, a plain white background, and the edge of the frame, which left expression and posture to carry the picture. Footage of him directing sitters and marking up contact sheets, which the trailer previews, is hard to find anywhere else. It sits alongside his earlier documentaries about Luciano Pavarotti, the Beatles, and Jim Henson, all portraits of artists at work.

articles.title: In 1839, a Philadelphian Took One of the First Selfies Ever Made
articles.summary: The plate is a daguerreotype, made in the fall of 1839, and it is one of the oldest surviving photographic portraits taken in the United States. Lead image: Robert Cornelius, self-portrait, October or November 1839.
articles.summary_short: The plate is a daguerreotype, made in the fall of 1839, and it is one of the oldest surviving photographic portraits taken in the United States. Lead image: Robert Cornelius, self-portrait, October or November 1839.
articles.summary_long:
A young man with tousled hair, a popped collar, and his arms loosely folded stares just past the lens, caught mid-thought in the daylight of a Philadelphia backyard. The plate is a daguerreotype, made in the fall of 1839, and it is one of the oldest surviving photographic portraits taken in the United States. His name was Robert Cornelius, and in October 1839 he was 30 years old.

His self-portrait was not the first photograph in America and it was not the first photograph of anything. What is documented is what he went back to. By that strict standard, nothing made in 1839 can be a selfie, and the honest description of Cornelius's plate is the museum one, what the Library of Congress calls the earliest extant American photographic portrait, which happens to be a self-portrait.

Cornelius even left his own account of the moment. His has an inscription in his own hand, a national archive behind it, and a documented life around it. Lead image: Robert Cornelius, self-portrait, October or November 1839.

articles.summary: A color darkroom print starts with a negative, an enlarger with a color head, and a sheet of RA-4 paper that won't show you what you got until it comes out of the chemistry. articles.summary_long:
A color darkroom print starts with a negative, an enlarger with a color head, and a sheet of RA-4 paper that won't show you what you got until it comes out of the chemistry. Most color film shot today ends its life as a lab scan, so printing it by hand puts the color balance and density decisions back in your own hands. His main tool is a De Vere 504 enlarger , which takes negatives up to 5x4 and has cyan, magenta, and yellow dials on its color head.

Paper goes through a Durst RCP 20 roller processor. The first strip lands close, though it runs a little dark and a little too magenta. Brightening it means less exposure time, so he drops to 9.5 seconds, and cutting magenta in the print means dialing more magenta into the head, so he goes from 92 to 95.

McDougall works through three test strips and two full prints before settling on 93 magenta, 74 yellow, 10 seconds, and f/16, a filter pack that falls between his second and third strips. His third strip adds a 1.3-second warm pre-flash, a brief exposure of the paper under a second enlarger, which shows up most in the window highlights. An exterior printed with the interior settings comes very close on the first strip, with the exposure right and a bit too much magenta, and the final print lands at 105 magenta.

articles.title: Navigate the Open Sea with Juliet Schreckinger’s Cooperative Creatures
articles.summary: Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, Juliet Schreckinger ’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Limitless Sea continues through November 29 in Philadelphia.
articles.summary_short: Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, Juliet Schreckinger ’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Limitless Sea continues through November 29 in Philadelphia.
articles.summary_long:
Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, Juliet Schreckinger ’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Personalities like Oscar the Octopus and Quinn the Sperm Whale recur in the artist’s ink and graphite drawings , and her most recent series comprises the show Limitless Sea at Arch Enemy Arts . Schreckinger’s marine and woodland critters adopt a playful, cartoonish air, like personalities in a children’s book who find themselves adrift and in need of a friend.

Lighthouses, lanterns, and rays of sun breaking through clouds glow with optimism. An undercurrent of persistence and hope also runs through Limited Sea , mirroring the artist’s recent healing process after a major surgery. It’s “a show made up of characters navigating through the foggy darkness by focusing on the light…and on the other side is limitless possibility,” Schreckinger says in a statement.

As she navigated her own challenges—including making this series with only one good eye—these works served as a reminder of what’s most important: “finding the beauty, finding the light, and spending time with those who make your soul happy,” she says. Limitless Sea continues through November 29 in Philadelphia. Schreckinger’s work will also be on view next month in General Strike 2 , an exhibition of artist matchboxes, at Joy Machine .

articles.title: Galaxy Outflows Likely Regulate Star Formation At ‘Cosmic Noon’ NASA’s Webb Reveals
articles.summary: But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.
articles.summary_short: But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.
articles.summary_long:
Sitting here on the outskirts of our Milky Way Galaxy, itâs hard to imagine the galactic machinations that led to our goldilocks spot around a very welcoming yellow dwarf star. But for decades, astronomers have suspected that the internal dynamics of massive galaxies like ours play an outsized role in regulating star formation. But such outflows likely remove a large quantity of gas from galaxies, which are then unable to form new stars.

Quenching can happen if the galaxy runs out of gas or the galaxy stops being able to turn the gas into stars because the gas is too hot or turbulent to collapse, says Davies. One possibility is that the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy releases a large amount of energy which removes and/or heats the gas and prevents the formation of new stars, says Belli. A key open question is what triggers outflows powerful enough to quench galaxies.

Outflows are very common in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, but most of these galaxies are not quenching: the outflows simply keep the galaxies in equilibrium and prevent them from converting all their gas into stars too quickly, says Davies. Possible triggers of the most powerful outflows include galaxy mergers, or radio jets launched by the central supermassive black holes, she says. When galaxies are quenched, the formation of new stars and planets is shut down, with strong repercussions on the probability of developing habitable systems, says Belli.

articles.title: Ringing Black Holes Offer Precision Tests of Relativity
articles.summary: Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally canât be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star.

articles.summary_long:
Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally canât be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. Adding to their mystery, several types of black holes exist, including free-floating black holes that drift independently throughout space, stellar-mass and are produced from exploding stars, and supermassive black holes that exist at the center of galaxies like our own.

But arguably one of the most mind-blowing mysteries about black holes is figuring out what happens when they collide, and even merge. Now, a team of more than 70 researchers might be one step closer to solving this decades-long conundrum as they used a combination of computer models and a literature review to analyze how black holes behave when they collide, specifically focusing on a well-known âringingâ phenomenon that occurs when black holes collide and merge. In a recent study published in Classical and Quantum Gravity, the primary motivation behind the study was to advance black hole research by establishing a long-known method called black hole spectroscopy from a theoretical concept to a practical one.

Black hole spectroscopy involves measuring the gravitational waves that are produced from two black holes colliding and merging, specifically focusing on the âringdownâ phase, or the waves produced from the newly merged black hole. And it wasnât for another 51 years that gravitational waves were first detected, 100 years after Einstein first proposed their existence in mathematical equations. What new insights into ringing black holes will researchers make in the coming years and decades?

A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. That means it's happening in a binary star, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.

In type Ia supernova, a white dwarf, called the accretor star, draws material away from another star called the donor star. A type Ia supernova can also occur in a double white dwarf binary, where the two stars merge and explode. This supernova is named SN 2026ahvu, where the suffix ahvu is a chronological identifier.

It signifies that the supernova is the 41,855th transient discovered in 2026. articles.title: This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?
articles.summary: But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.

articles.summary_long:
Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.

But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write.

The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. "We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.

articles.title: The Poignant Animation ‘Paper Trail’ Chronicles a Life in Handwriting
articles.summary: From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by Don Hertzfeldt , the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school.

articles.summary_long:
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by Don Hertzfeldt , the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.

Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The film is available for streaming for a limited-timed on Vimeo , along with more of Hertzfeldt’s work.

articles.title: Practice Mindfulness with Roeselien Raimond’s Portraits of Relaxed Winter Foxes
articles.summary: Winter may not be everyone’s favorite, and it’s easy to dwell on gray days and leafless trees. It’s a side of the season that photographer Roeselien Raimond expresses in her series Zen & The Art of Winter Foxes .
articles.summary_short: Winter may not be everyone’s favorite, and it’s easy to dwell on gray days and leafless trees. It’s a side of the season that photographer Roeselien Raimond expresses in her series Zen & The Art of Winter Foxes .
articles.summary_long:
Come November and December, northerly climes brace for dropping temperatures and the first snow. Winter may not be everyone’s favorite, and it’s easy to dwell on gray days and leafless trees. Fortunately, when the sun shines, the cold months can also reveal abundant life and beauty, and many woodland denizens thrive during this time of the year.

It’s a side of the season that photographer Roeselien Raimond expresses in her series Zen & The Art of Winter Foxes . Raimond documents serene vulpine creatures in moments of repose amid peaceful, snowy surrounds. “The images are part of a personal project about the unexpected connection between nature, photography and inner peace,” the artist tells Colossal.

“The idea originated from an encounter with a vixen during a snowstorm, when I found myself feeling completely at ease despite the freezing conditions.” Meeting the reclusive animal spurred an ongoing series and exploration of the Zen paradox of desire , in which the search for something can make it more difficult to find. Raimond taps into nature’s powerful lesson that quietude and mindfulness can help us to recharge, just like the foxes’ natural inclination to rest, reflect, and simply soak up some rays.

Conjure an image of a basket in your mind. Is it made of straw, or perhaps sweetgrass or willow? At Mindy Solomon Gallery , a forthcoming exhibition titled Interwoven: Basketry As Expanded Practice challenges our perception of both object and craft.

This vibrant survey “breaks craft tradition,” Clements says, positioning the practice as an art form. The show asks “what happens when basketry is understood not as a fixed category of craft, but as an open-ended artistic language?” The artists in Interwoven use a range of materials, from ceramic and steel to cotton and paper. Salvador Dominguez ’s vibrant pipe cleaner vessels are complemented by wall works like Eric Gushee ’s intricately interlaced wire sculptures and Miguel Arzabe ’s woven, deconstructed paintings.

Viewers will find further explorations by artists like Dienke Dekker and José Santiago Pérez , who work with unexpected materials like paper and emergency blankets, respectively. And Colossal readers might also recognize work by Xanthe Somers and Sonia Barrett , among the nearly two dozen participating artists. Interwoven opens on November 29 and continues through January 9 in Miami.

Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds -- and some then explode .

Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right -- in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas.

Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.

articles.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
articles.summary: Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers. On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round.

articles.summary_long:
Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers. On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers.

Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania. An aerial survey planned for December should yield an estimate of how much ice remains in 2026, Permana said. By November 2024, the ice at this site was gone.

Puncak Jaya’s remaining ice has thinned so much and broken into such small, stagnant patches that it no longer flows. “While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said. As for the remaining patches of ice, time will tell how long they last.

Radial distortion is normally written as a polynomial in the distance from the center of the frame. The manual Distortion slider in Camera Raw and Lightroom is one number. Photoshop's Lens Correction filter gives you one Remove Distortion value.

articles.title: Two Hard-Light Portrait Looks From One Strobe and a Plain White Wall
articles.summary: Soft light gets most of the credit in portrait work, yet a single snooted or bare strobe can give you crisp shadows, graphic shapes, and a sense of depth that a big softbox tends to smooth away. articles.summary_long:
Soft light gets most of the credit in portrait work, yet a single snooted or bare strobe can give you crisp shadows, graphic shapes, and a sense of depth that a big softbox tends to smooth away. If you're working with one strobe and a white wall, hard light is one of the quickest ways to make a small setup look deliberate and layered. Nathan Elson uses one anyway and pulls two very different portrait looks out of it with a single light.

Distance is one of the most useful levers you have with hard light, and it pays to understand what it changes. With a strobe 5 ft from a standing person, her head and her knees can sit at noticeably different distances from the light, and you'll see a clear brightness gradient down her body. Moving the light back also makes it smaller relative to the subject, which keeps shadow edges crisp.

You can apply this to any full-length hard-light portrait. Elson moves the light to camera left, roughly 15 ft from the model, aiming for light that hits the top and bottom halves of her body evenly. The angle is set so the left side of her face falls into shadow for drama, while the shadow her body casts gets pushed out of the frame, leaving a clean white background.

Le 30 octobre, l’action Intel a plongé de 28,6 %, après la publication de prévisions trimestrielles inférieures aux attentes de Wall Street. Pour le quatrième trimestre 2026, le fabricant anticipait un chiffre d’affaires compris entre 15 et 16 milliards de dollars. Intel a enregistré un chiffre d’affaires de 16,5 milliards de dollars, en hausse de 21 % sur un an.

La correction boursière a entraîné une perte d’environ 140 milliards de dollars de valorisation. La plainte évoque également une levée de fonds de 23 milliards de dollars réalisée en août, à 95 dollars par action. Malgré la récente correction, l’action Intel affichait encore une progression de 62 % depuis le début de l’année au 13 novembre, à 59,66 dollars.

articles.summary_long:
SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test. The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. "Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot said.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September . SpaceX said the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. SpaceX plans to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana .

Photoshop 2027 and the Camera Raw update that came with it add a long list of features, with more already waiting in the Photoshop beta, and many of them draw on Adobe's generative credits, so plenty of clicks now carry a cost on top of your subscription. Knowing which tools hold up at full resolution and which ones soften your files decides whether an update speeds up your editing or adds cleanup work. Until now, Camera Raw's AI noise reduction only worked on raw files.

Remove Related Elements costs 10 credits, and Enhance adds 10 more, or 20 on files over 25 megapixels. That pattern holds for nearly every generative tool in Photoshop, and you can apply it on your own. A practical habit is to sort features into two groups before you use them: tools that analyze the pixels you already have, like Denoise, and tools that create new pixels.

If the hover behavior bothers you, both changes can be turned off under Settings > Interface. Quick Compare shows a before-and-after split with one click, and its "before" is the file as you opened it in the current session, so after you save and reopen, it only tracks the changes you make from that point. In Camera Raw, you can now copy AI removals from one photo to others through Copy and Paste Edit Settings, though you may need to drag a removal back into place if the framing shifted between shots.

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination. There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions , which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe.

Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these.

Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins? But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. One 2022 study, titled " Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes ," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.

Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments.

articles.summary: Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory . The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson.

articles.summary_long:
Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory . The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson. To create the film, Doran attributed various pinks and reds to different wavelengths, creating an alluring interpretation of the fiery orb.

Doran stitched together NASA’s captures, or more accurately, he says, the images were “conformed, repaired, graded, blended, rescaled and retimed” into a seamless film. “Crimson Star” is one of several astral projects he’s undertaken in recent years, and you can keep up with his latest works on YouTube .

articles.summary_long:
Prévu pour l’été 2027, l’International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence (ICAID) réunira plusieurs pays alliés pour travailler sur le développement, l’évaluation et l’interopérabilité des systèmes d’IA militaires. La France entend renforcer sa position dans le domaine de l’IA militaire. Le ministère des Armées a annoncé, le 12 novembre 2026, la création de l’International Center for Artificial Intelligence in Defence (ICAID).

Installé à Rennes, ce centre doit réunir des experts de plusieurs pays partenaires autour des enjeux de conception, d’acquisition, de déploiement et d’évaluation des technologies d’IA destinées aux forces armées. L’ICAID ne développera pas directement de services d’IA destinés aux armées. Le centre devrait compter au minimum 34 personnels civils et militaires, dont 17 Français.

Alors que l’AMIAD se concentre sur le développement et le déploiement de solutions d’intelligence artificielle au profit des forces françaises, l’ICAID aura pour vocation de renforcer la coopération internationale et de favoriser l’adoption de méthodes communes entre pays partenaires. Avec l’ICAID, la France ajoute ainsi une dimension internationale à sa stratégie d’IA de défense. Le centre doit atteindre sa capacité opérationnelle à l’été 2027.

On pense que ce phénomène est gouverné par une énergie noire exotique dont la nature et la variabilité sont inconnues. Plusieurs scénarios sont possibles comme celui d'une modification future de l'énergie noire provoquant une fin de l'expansion dans un futur pas trop lointain, suivie d'une contraction en route vers un nouveau Big Bang.

Les secrets de cette énergie noire, et donc le destin du cosmos, pourraient être révélés en utilisant le satellite Euclid et sa capacité à mesurer comme jamais depuis environ 10 milliards d'années les variations de l'expansion de l'espace. Les premiers résultats scientifiques d'Euclid sur cette route, qui permet aussi d'étudier la matière noire et d'autres questions d'astrophysique et de cosmologie, sont révélés aujourd'hui par l'Esa....
